name: Gene Sharp
bio: Gene Sharp was an American political scientist and the foremost scholar of nonviolent struggle, founder of the Albert Einstein Institution, whose writings influenced anti-authoritarian resistance movements around the world. As a young pacifist he refused conscription during the Korean War: convicted of draft refusal, he was sentenced to two years and served nine months in federal prison in 1953-54, corresponding from prison with Albert Einstein (who wrote the foreword to his first book) about his decision to go to prison for his beliefs.
charges: Refusing conscription (draft refusal) during the Korean War
sentence: Two-year sentence; served nine months in federal prison (1953-54)

name: Eve Tetaz
bio: Eve Tetaz was a retired Washington, D.C. public school teacher who became a prominent peace-and-justice activist, repeatedly committing nonviolent civil resistance against the Iraq War, torture, and the Guantanamo detentions. Arrested some eleven times in 2007 alone and roughly a dozen more times in 2008-2010, she refused to pay fines and served a series of jail sentences — including 7 days (2007), 5 days (2008), 25 days (2010), and 60 days in the D.C. Jail after a 2012 banner protest at the U.S. Supreme Court. She was active with Code Pink, the National Campaign for Nonviolent Resistance, and Witness Against Torture.
charges: Nonviolent civil resistance — anti-war, anti-torture, and Guantanamo protests (unlawful assembly / disorderly conduct / failure to obey)
sentence: Served repeated jail terms (e.g. 7, 5, 25, and 60 days) for refusing fines and probation

name: Ron Kovic
bio: Ron Kovic is a U.S. Marine Corps sergeant who was paralyzed from the chest down in the Vietnam War and became one of the country's most visible anti-war activists, author of the 1976 memoir Born on the Fourth of July. A leader in Vietnam Veterans Against the War, he was arrested roughly a dozen times in nonviolent anti-war protests beginning in 1971 — including occupying a California draft-board office — and served jail time for the demonstrations.
charges: Nonviolent anti-war civil disobedience (trespass / refusing to disperse) — draft-board and other protests
convicted: Arrested about a dozen times (from 1971); jailed for the protests
sentence: Served jail time for repeated anti-war demonstrations

name: Stew Albert
bio: Stew Albert was an early member of the Yippies (Youth International Party) and a key figure in the 1960s New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement. He was incarcerated, under the supervision of the Alameda County sheriff, during the Vietnam Day Committee's anti-draft protests in downtown Oakland, California; he was later arrested at the 1968 Democratic National Convention and named an unindicted co-conspirator in the Chicago Seven case.
charges: Anti-draft / anti-war protest — the Vietnam Day Committee demonstrations, Oakland, California
convicted: Jailed during the Vietnam Day Committee anti-draft protests (1965-66)
sentence: Incarceration during the Oakland anti-draft protests
